title: Design Strava / fitness activity tracking
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, offline upload, processing pipeline, segments and leaderboards, feed, privacy, storage tiering.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Strava records your run or ride from your phone or watch (GPS points plus heart rate, cadence, power), stores it as an activity, computes stats, and shows it to your followers. The social part (feed, kudos, segments, leaderboards) is what makes it more than a stopwatch. Garmin Connect, Nike Run Club, Komoot and Apple Fitness share the shape.

Functional requirements

  • Record an activity on a device (works offline), upload when online.
  • Process: distance, pace, elevation, heart-rate zones, map polyline, splits.
  • Segments: a named stretch of road; rank everyone's time on it (leaderboards).
  • Follow athletes, activity feed, kudos and comments; privacy zones (hide start/end near home).
  • Import from watches and third-party devices (FIT/GPX files).

Non-functional requirements

  • Never lose an activity (a 3-hour ride is irreplaceable); uploads are retry-safe.
  • Processing within seconds to a couple of minutes; real-time is not required.
  • Reads (feed, maps) far outnumber uploads.
  • Spiky: weekends and morning, January resolutions, big events.

Decision gravity. Treat the raw upload as an immutable source of truth and every derived number (stats, segment efforts, maps) as recomputable. When your segment-matching algorithm improves, you can reprocess. Storing only derived values is a one-way door; you could never fix a bug.

Everyday analogy. A diary where you keep the original receipts and compute the monthly totals from them.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing live GPS streaming when the product mostly uploads finished activities.
  • Forgetting offline recording and flaky uploads.
  • Ignoring privacy (publishing home location).

notes.title: API
notes.html:
POST /v1/uploads                       // step 1: create an upload session
{ "fileName": "ride.fit", "sizeBytes": 1840000, "sha256": "ab12...", "source": "garmin" }
201 { "uploadId": "u_77", "uploadUrl": "https://storage.example/presigned?...", "chunkSize": 1048576 }

PUT  <uploadUrl>   (client uploads bytes straight to object storage; Range-resumable)
POST /v1/uploads/u_77/complete  -> 202 { "activityId": "a_5001", "status": "PROCESSING" }
GET /v1/activities/a_5001
200 { "id":"a_5001", "type":"ride", "distanceM":42180, "movingTimeS":5230, "elevationGainM":412,
      "avgHr":148, "polyline":"encoded...", "splits":[...], "segmentEfforts":[...], "privacy":"followers" }

GET /v1/feed?cursor=...&limit=20       -> list of activities from followed athletes
POST /v1/activities/a_5001/kudos       -> 204 (idempotent)
GET /v1/segments/s_9/leaderboard?filter=this_month&limit=10
GET /v1/athletes/me/activities?from=2026-10-01

Streams for a detailed chart come separately and are cacheable:

GET /v1/activities/a_5001/streams?keys=latlng,altitude,heartrate&resolution=medium
200 { "latlng": [[12.97,77.59], ...], "altitude":[...], "heartrate":[...] }

The two-step presigned upload keeps big bytes off your API servers. sha256 plus uploadId makes retries and duplicate files harmless.

Industry example. Strava's public API v3 exposes activities, streams, segments and uploads with exactly this shape (activity summary vs streams).

Everyday analogy. Posting a parcel: you get a tracking number first, then hand over the parcel at a drop point.

Common interview traps.

  • Sending 2 MB of GPS through the API server instead of presigned storage URLs.
  • Returning full streams in the list endpoint.
  • No idempotency on uploads (duplicate activities after a retry).

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 100M registered, 20M monthly active, 5M activities/day at peak design.

Quantity Calculation Result
Uploads 5M / 86,400 ~58/s avg, peak ~300/s (weekend mornings)
Raw file 1 hour at 1 point/s: 3,600 points x ~30 B (compressed FIT) ~100 KB to 2 MB
Raw storage/day 5M x 500 KB avg 2.5 TB/day, ~900 TB/year
Derived record summary + polyline ~10 KB 50 GB/day
Streams (parsed) 3,600 pts x 5 channels x 4 B ~72 KB per hour, compressible
Feed reads 20M MAU x 5 opens/day x 3 (peak) / 86,400 ~3,500/s
Segment efforts 5M activities x ~5 segments 25M efforts/day (~290/s)

What this tells you. Throughput is small (hundreds of uploads per second). Storage is large (about a petabyte per year raw), so use object storage with lifecycle tiering (hot 90 days, then cheaper class). Compute is bursty and CPU-heavy per activity (parsing, map matching), a queue-plus-workers pattern.

Everyday analogy. Few people hand in forms per minute, but every form is a thick folder.

Common interview traps.

  • Overbuilding for QPS while ignoring petabyte-scale storage cost.
  • Storing GPS points as rows (billions of rows) in a relational table.
  • Forgetting that segment matching multiplies work per activity.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Upload service: issues presigned URLs, tracks upload sessions, dedupes by hash.
  • Processing workers: parse FIT/GPX/TCX, clean noise (GPS jitter, auto-pause), compute distance (haversine on the smoothed track), elevation (use a terrain DEM instead of noisy barometer/GPS altitude when needed), splits, zones.
  • Activity DB: metadata and summaries. Postgres sharded by athlete id (an athlete's activities are read together), or Cassandra with (athlete_id, start_time) partitioning.
  • Stream store: parsed time series in compressed columnar blobs in object storage, or Cassandra/Timescale for time-based queries.
  • Segment service: matches tracks to segments; maintains leaderboards.
  • Feed service: fan-out of finished activities to followers (see news feed design).

Decision gravity. Choose partition key athlete_id for activities: 95% of reads are "an athlete's activities". It breaks for global queries ("all activities in this area for heatmaps"), which you serve from a separate derived store. Partition key change is a one-way door in effort.

Industry examples. Strava has described using Cassandra, Postgres, and pipelines on Kafka plus Spark for its global heatmap; the heatmap aggregates billions of GPS points into tiles.

Everyday analogy. A mailroom (upload), a sorting floor (workers), and lockers per athlete (activity DB).

Common interview traps.

  • Synchronous processing inside the upload request.
  • One table with billions of GPS rows.
  • No backfill/reprocess path.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Offline recording and resumable upload

The phone stores points in a local SQLite (Android Room) as they arrive, with a periodic flush (every 10 s) so a crash loses little. Keep GPS sampling 1 Hz with smart pausing to save battery (about 5 to 8%/hour is typical for GPS-heavy apps).

On finish: write a local file, create an upload session, upload chunks of 1 MB with Content-Range; if the network drops, ask the server which bytes it has and resume. The completion call is idempotent: complete(uploadId) twice yields the same activity.

Use WorkManager on Android for guaranteed, constraint-aware retries (unmetered network). Deduplicate by content hash: if the user syncs the same ride from both the watch and the phone, the second one is detected as a duplicate (same start time and near-identical distance) and merged or flagged.

Decision gravity. Idempotent upload sessions are cheap now and impossible to bolt on later (after you have duplicates in the DB). Reversible policy: dedupe thresholds.

Everyday analogy. Carrying water in a bucket relay: if someone drops out, you know how many buckets already reached the tank.

Common interview traps.

  • Re-uploading a full file after a 90% interruption.
  • No local persistence (app killed means ride lost).
  • Server-side duplicates when a user taps "Save" twice.

Processing pipeline

  1. Parse FIT/GPX/TCX into points (t, lat, lng, alt, hr, cadence, power).
  2. Clean: drop impossible speeds (over 40 m/s on foot), snap short gaps, Kalman or Douglas-Peucker smoothing; detect auto-pause (speed under 0.5 m/s for 10 s).
  3. Metrics: distance = sum of haversine between smoothed points; elevation gain with a threshold (ignore changes under 3 m to avoid noise inflating gain); normalised power and training load for cycling.
  4. Publish: write summary to DB, streams to storage, emit activity.processed event.

Workers are stateless consumers of a Kafka topic (partition count 24 to 48, key by activity id); a failed message retries with backoff and then goes to a dead-letter queue. Make every stage idempotent (write by activity id, overwrite on rerun).

Production incident pattern. Symptom: stats look wrong for a whole batch of activities (distance too high). Metric: distribution of distance/duration against previous day. Cause: a smoothing parameter change. Fix: because raw is immutable, bump pipeline version and reprocess the affected range.

Decision gravity. Store pipelineVersion on each derived record. It makes reprocessing a routine operation (two-way door) instead of a crisis.

Everyday analogy. A factory line: each station does one job, and a defective batch can be rerun from the raw material.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing GPS altitude is accurate.
  • Non-idempotent workers that double count on retry.
  • Summing raw point distances (zig-zag noise inflates the total).

Segments and leaderboards

A segment is a polyline (start line, end line) such as a hill climb. For each new activity, find segments it passes through and compute the elapsed time.

Matching at scale (millions of segments, millions of activities):

  1. Spatial pre-filter: index segments by geo cells (S2/H3/geohash). For an activity, collect its cells (a 1-hour ride crosses maybe 200 cells), fetch candidate segments in those cells (hundreds, not millions).
  2. Precise match: for each candidate, check the track passes within ~15 m of the start point, then follows the segment path (compare direction and distance to the segment polyline), then passes the end; effort time = interpolated time at end minus time at start.
  3. Store effort (segment_id, athlete_id, activity_id, elapsedS, date).

Leaderboards: Redis sorted set per segment per scope, ZADD segment:9:alltime elapsedS athlete. Keep the best effort per athlete (ZADD LT to keep only a lower score in Redis 6.2+). Top 10: ZRANGE ... 0 9; "my rank": ZRANK. Variants (this year, age group, friends) are separate sets or computed at read time from smaller sets. Popular segments have millions of efforts; sorted sets handle around 10M members per key but memory is about 100 B per member, so 1 GB per popular segment (tier the rest into a database).

Decision gravity. Efforts DB is the source of truth; Redis leaderboards are caches rebuildable from it, so you can change the leaderboard tech. Accuracy rules (how strict is "followed the segment") affect fairness and cheating; changing them means recomputing history, which is expensive but possible with raw data.

Everyday analogy. Every athlete is timed on the same marked stretch of road, and a scoreboard shows the best time per person.

Common interview traps.

  • Checking every activity against every segment.
  • Counting a car-assisted "ride" (add speed sanity checks and flagging).
  • Updating leaderboards in the upload request.

Feed and privacy

On activity.processed, push the activity id to followers' feeds. Most athletes have under 500 followers, so fan-out on write into per-follower Redis lists is fine; for pros with millions of followers use pull-on-read merge (the same hybrid as the news feed design). Feed item = id only; the card is hydrated from the activity cache.

Privacy zones. Athletes define a radius (for example 200 m) around home/work. When serving the public polyline and streams to others, trim points inside the zone. Do it on the read path with a per-viewer visibility check, or precompute a public version of the polyline at processing time and store both (private and public), because security bugs in per-request trimming leak addresses. Strava's 2018 global heatmap incident showed that aggregated data can reveal military base layouts, so aggregate with minimum thresholds and respect opt-out.

Decision gravity. Precomputing a public derivative is a one-way door only if you forget to store it; the benefit is safety by construction. Default new users to the safest setting.

Everyday analogy. Blurring the front door in a photo before you post it.

Common interview traps.

  • Hiding start/end only in the UI while the API returns raw points.
  • Fan-out to all followers of a celebrity on every activity.
  • Using activity-level privacy but forgetting segment leaderboards (they expose names and times).

Maps, heatmaps and storage tiering

Render maps from the polyline: store a Google-encoded polyline (about 5 to 10 KB for a ride) and a thumbnail image; serve tiles from a CDN. The global heatmap: a batch job (Spark) bins points into map tiles at zoom levels 0 to 16 (z/x/y), counts per pixel, normalises, writes PNG tiles to object storage with CDN in front; refresh weekly or monthly.

Storage lifecycle: raw files 0 to 90 days on standard storage, 90 days to 1 year infrequent-access, after that archive class (S3 Glacier). Keep the derived records hot. Cost of 1 PB in S3 Standard is roughly 23 USD/TB-month (confirm current pricing), so tiering saves a lot.

Decision gravity. Archiving raw data trades cost against reprocessing speed. Reversible by policy but retrieval from archive takes hours, so keep recent raw data hot.

Everyday analogy. Putting old photo albums in the attic but keeping the recent ones on the shelf.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing heatmaps in real time from the OLTP DB.
  • Not tiering storage and paying a petabyte at the top price.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Clear separation of upload, processing, serving.
  • Numbers: low QPS, huge storage; why object storage and presigned uploads.
  • Immutable raw plus recomputable derived data and pipeline versioning.
  • Segment matching with a spatial pre-filter, and leaderboards in sorted sets backed by a durable store.
  • Idempotency across upload, workers and kudos.
  • Privacy and abuse (zones, cheating, GDPR delete across raw, derived, caches).
  • Seniors discuss offline-first mobile design, battery, schema evolution, cost tiering.

Common interview traps.

  • Real-time streaming architecture for a mostly batch workflow.
  • Skipping privacy.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Activity = immutable raw file plus derived, recomputable records; store a pipeline version.
  • Upload with presigned, resumable, idempotent sessions; process via Kafka and stateless workers.
  • Throughput is small (hundreds of uploads/s), storage is huge (about a PB/year): object storage plus lifecycle tiers.
  • Partition activities by athlete; keep streams in compressed blobs, not one row per GPS point.
  • Segments: geo-cell pre-filter, then precise matching; leaderboards in Redis sorted sets over a durable efforts table.
  • Feed uses hybrid fan-out; privacy zones are enforced by precomputed public derivatives.

questions.promptHtml: Why keep the raw uploaded file as an immutable source of truth and treat stats, segment efforts and maps as derived data?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you design for reprocessing, because algorithms and bugs change over time.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A ride is irreplaceable, and my smoothing, elevation and segment-matching code will change. If I store only derived numbers, a bug or an improvement can never be fixed. So I keep the original FIT/GPX file in object storage untouched, and every derived record (distance, elevation, efforts, polylines) can be recomputed from it. I also stamp each derived record with a pipelineVersion, so reprocessing a range is routine instead of a crisis.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Device -> presigned upload -> Object storage (raw, immutable)
                           -> Kafka -> workers -> Activity DB (derived, versioned)
                                               -> Stream store, efforts, leaderboards

Derived data is cheap to recompute relative to losing the original. Workers are idempotent (write by activity id, overwrite on rerun), so reprocess is safe. The cost is storage: roughly 2.5 TB/day raw at 5M activities a day, so lifecycle tiering matters.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing only the computed summary.
  • Designing live GPS streaming when the product mostly uploads finished activities.
  • Forgetting offline recording and flaky uploads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does pipelineVersion buy you? -> Find and rerun exactly the records produced by a buggy version.
  2. What about GDPR delete? -> Delete raw, derived, caches and leaderboard entries; plan for it from the start.
  3. Cost of keeping raw forever? -> Tier to infrequent access and archive after 90 days and a year.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "store the activity in the DB". Senior: raw plus recomputable derived, idempotent workers, versioning and tiering.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A smoothing change inflated distances; because raw files were kept, the affected range was reprocessed in a night.

questions.promptHtml: With millions of segments and millions of activities per day, how do you find which segments an activity passed through without checking every pair?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests spatial pre-filtering and precise matching as two stages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I index segments by geo cell (S2, H3 or geohash). For each activity I collect the cells its track crosses (a one-hour ride is maybe 200 cells), fetch the few hundred candidate segments in those cells, and only then do precise matching: the track must pass within about 15 m of the segment start, follow the segment path (direction and distance), and reach the end. Elapsed time is interpolated time at the end minus at the start, stored as an effort.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity track -> cells covered (~200) -> candidate segments (~hundreds) -> precise match -> efforts DB -> leaderboards

Matching work per activity is hundreds of candidates, not millions. At 5M activities x ~5 segments that is about 25M efforts per day (about 290/s). It runs in the asynchronous processing workers, never in the upload request.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Checking every activity against every segment.
  • Not checking direction or path, so a car-assisted drive-by counts.
  • Updating leaderboards inside the upload request.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. GPS noise at the start line? -> Tolerance radius (about 15 m) and time interpolation between points.
  2. Cheating by car? -> Speed sanity checks and flagging.
  3. New segment created later? -> Backfill by scanning activities in its cells from the stored tracks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "loop over segments". Senior: cell pre-filter, candidate count math, precise match rules, async processing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A naive matcher scaled with segments x activities and starved the processing queue every Sunday morning.

questions.contextHtml: 5M activities/day, average raw file 500 KB. The CFO asks why storage is 40 percent of the bill. Today everything is in the standard object storage class with no lifecycle. Assume list prices of about 23 USD/TB-month standard, about 12.5 infrequent access, and about 4 archive (verify current pricing). Old raw files are read rarely (reprocessing, user export).
questions.promptHtml: Do the capacity math and propose a lifecycle policy with its risks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compress it" without numbers, or archive everything immediately.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Retention requirement? How often is old raw read? Retrieval time tolerance?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable a lifecycle rule now; it applies to existing objects.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Storage cost dominated by cold data in the top tier.
  4. How I'd verify each: Storage metrics by age; access logs of raw reads by age.
  5. Root cause: 5M x 500 KB = 2.5 TB/day, about 900 TB/year; about 1 PB at 23 USD/TB-month is roughly 23,000 USD per month, growing every month.
  6. Fix: Raw: 0 to 90 days standard (225 TB, about 5,200 USD/month), 90 days to 1 year infrequent access, then archive. After a year, with 900 TB: about 225 TB hot, 675 TB cold. If cold is archive at 4 USD/TB-month that is about 2,700 USD instead of 15,500 at standard: total about 7,900 versus 20,700 per month. Keep derived records and streams (about 50 GB/day) hot. Compress parsed streams in columnar blobs.
  7. Prevention: Cost dashboard by prefix and age; alert on growth slope; lifecycle in IaC.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Archive retrieval takes hours and costs per request, so reprocessing old data becomes slow and not free; keep the last 90 days hot. Minimum storage durations apply on cold classes (verify).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Dedupe identical files? -> Content hash dedupe saves duplicates from watch and phone syncs.
  • User asks for old activity map? -> Derived polyline stays hot, so it renders instantly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Storage grew linearly for two years with no lifecycle; a one-day rule change cut the monthly bill by more than half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Compression only.
  • Hire: TB/day and tiering math.
  • Strong hire: Hot/cold split, retrieval trade-off, derived data stays hot, cost governance.

questions.contextHtml:
After a mobile release users report duplicate rides in their feed and doubled kudos. Metrics:

duplicate activities (same athlete, same start +/- 5 s, distance within 1%):  18,400 / day (was 600)
uploads/complete called twice with same uploadId:   31% of duplicates
ride synced from watch AND phone:                    58% of duplicates

The retry policy in the new app version retries complete on any timeout, without checking status.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this happen and how do you fix it at every layer?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a unique index on start time."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is complete idempotent server-side? Is the content hash used? How do we treat watch and phone copies of the same ride?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side dedupe job: merge activities with same athlete, near-identical start and distance, keep the richer source (watch with HR).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) complete creates a new activity per call; (b) two device sources produce separate uploads; (c) clients re-upload after a partial failure.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group duplicates by uploadId and by sha256; compare sources.
  5. Root cause: complete(uploadId) is not idempotent and there is no cross-source duplicate detection.
  6. Fix: Make complete idempotent: it returns the same activityId for the same uploadId (unique constraint). Dedupe by sha256 plus uploadId for exact repeats, and by heuristics (start time, distance) for cross-device copies with a merge or flag policy. Clients resume chunks by asking the server which bytes it has instead of re-uploading. Retry with backoff, and use the platform's guaranteed work scheduler (for example WorkManager on Android).
  7. Prevention: Duplicate-rate metric, contract test calling complete twice, canary release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Heuristic dedupe thresholds can merge two genuine back-to-back rides; make the policy reversible (flag first, merge later). I would not delete duplicates silently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not rely on a unique index on start time? -> Different devices have different clock offsets and sampling.
  • Idempotency key lifetime? -> Keep the upload session record for at least as long as clients can retry (days).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "Save" button double-fire produced 4,000 duplicate rides in a day; idempotent sessions would have turned them into harmless repeats.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Unique index on a timestamp.
  • Hire: Idempotent complete and hash dedupe.
  • Strong hire: Cross-device heuristics with reversible policy, resumable uploads, client retry rules, metrics.

questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem: for six days after pipeline v41 shipped, running distances were 3 to 5 percent high and elevation gain 30 percent high for about 4.2M activities. Athletes noticed personal records they could not reproduce. Metric review:

distance/duration ratio (daily median):  v40 = 3.02 m/s   v41 = 3.17 m/s
elevation gain per km (median):          v40 = 9 m        v41 = 12 m
change in v41: smoothing window 5 -> 1 point, elevation threshold 3 m -> 0 m

The change passed unit tests because tests used clean synthetic tracks.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: detection, repair and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert and hope." No repair of the 4.2M, no explanation of why tests missed it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is raw immutable? Do leaderboards and PRs depend on these numbers? Do we store pipeline version per record?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to v40, stop publishing new v41 records.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Parameter change in smoothing and elevation threshold; GPS jitter now counted as distance (zig-zag) and altitude noise counted as gain.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-run a sample of raw files on both versions, diff distance and elevation; look at the noise spectrum.
  5. Root cause: Summing haversine over unsmoothed points inflates distance; a 0 m elevation threshold counts every noise wiggle as climb.
  6. Fix: Bump to v42 with fixed parameters and reprocess the affected range, selected by pipelineVersion = 41, from the immutable raw files through the Kafka-backed workers (idempotent overwrites). Recompute segment efforts and leaderboards from the efforts table; send activity.reprocessed events so caches refresh. Notify users whose records changed.
  7. Prevention: Distribution monitors (distance/duration, gain per km) with day-over-day alerts; golden-file tests with real noisy tracks; staged rollout to 1 percent of uploads with metric gates.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Reprocessing 4.2M activities is CPU-heavy: throttle it so live uploads keep their SLA. I would not edit values in place without versions or backups.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PRs awarded under v41? -> Recompute from efforts; invalidated PRs removed with a notice.
  • Why is GPS altitude unreliable? -> Noisy; use a terrain model or barometer and thresholds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A smoothing tweak silently added 4 percent to every run for a week; the reprocess job was fine because raw was never touched.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Revert only.
  • Hire: Reprocess from raw by version.
  • Strong hire: Metric distribution alerts, noisy golden tests, staged rollout, throttled reprocess and user comms.

questions.contextHtml:
A journalist shows that an athlete's home address can be derived: the public activity map trims the first 200 m, but the streams endpoint returns raw latlng to followers, the segment Hill-Start-12 begins at the athlete's street and the public leaderboard lists name and time, and the "recent efforts" panel lists the segment. The privacy zone is only applied in the mobile UI.

GET /v1/activities/a_5001/streams?keys=latlng   -> first point 12.9716,77.5946 (home)
GET /v1/segments/s_9/leaderboard                -> "Priya K., 04:12"
questions.promptHtml: What failed, and how do you redesign so privacy is safe by construction?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Hide it in the UI" or only trims the polyline.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who may see streams (followers only, public, private)? Are efforts public by default? What zone radius options exist?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the streams endpoint for non-owners temporarily; hide efforts for segments starting inside any privacy zone.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Enforcement in the client only; several read paths (map, streams, efforts, leaderboard) not covered; aggregates revealing patterns.
  4. How I'd verify each: Call every read API as a follower and as an anonymous user and check for points inside zones; grep API responses for raw coordinates.
  5. Root cause: Privacy was a UI feature, not a data-layer property; each endpoint decided on its own.
  6. Fix: At processing time, precompute and store a public derivative (polyline and streams with zone points trimmed) beside the private version; the API serves public data to non-owners from a separate path, so there is nothing to leak by a per-request bug. Efforts on segments whose start or end lies inside the viewer-visible zone are excluded from public leaderboards or shown without identity. Default new users to the safest setting. Delete flows cover raw, derived, caches and leaderboards.
  7. Prevention: Automated privacy tests over every endpoint, red-team review, minimum-count thresholds on aggregates such as heatmaps.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The derivative doubles some storage, a small cost; changing a zone triggers reprocessing of past activities. I would not rely on per-request trimming alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User shrinks the zone later? -> Re-derive public copies from raw; old caches invalidated.
  • Heatmap risk? -> Aggregate with thresholds and respect opt-out; a global heatmap once exposed sensitive sites.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Home start points leaked through a feature added months after the privacy zones shipped; nobody had listed it as a read path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: UI-level hiding.
  • Hire: Server-side trimming on all read paths.
  • Strong hire: Precomputed public derivative, leaderboard/effort leakage, automated endpoint tests, deletion coverage.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "Add live tracking so family can watch my run in real time." The existing system is upload-after-finish, with 58 uploads/s average and a processing pipeline for finished files. Marketing expects 1M concurrent live sessions on New Year's Day.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond before drawing any boxes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Bolts WebSocket onto the upload API or starts designing with no questions.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who may watch (invited contacts only)? Required freshness (5 s? 30 s)? Is live data persisted or discarded? Battery budget? What happens when the phone loses signal? Do live sessions become normal activities afterwards?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I restate the requirement: ephemeral location sharing for invited viewers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: It is a second, separate system from the post-upload pipeline.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype with real battery tests; check viewer-to-athlete ratio (usually 1 to 5).
  5. Root cause: n/a; sizing: 1M sessions at a ping every 5 s = 200k writes/s, in-memory ephemeral store keyed by session with a short TTL; no durable write per ping.
  6. Fix (design): Persistent connection or lightweight pushes from phone; a live service keeps the latest point per session in memory/Redis and fans out to viewers with 1 to 5 s delay; adaptive rate when stationary; at finish the normal file upload happens and the session is closed. Viewer access via signed invite tokens with expiry; persist nothing except an optional low-rate trace if the user opts in.
  7. Prevention: Privacy review (stalking risk): easy stop, notifications to the athlete, auto-expire, no sharing with the public.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not reuse the upload path or store every ping in the activity DB; I would not promise real-time for everyone at launch without a load test.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Phone offline for 10 minutes? -> Viewers see "last seen"; the phone buffers and the final upload is authoritative.
  • Battery? -> Lower GPS/ping rate when slow; batch pings.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A live-share feature launched without expiry and a user kept sharing for weeks after a run; safety review added auto-stop.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Starts designing without questions.
  • Hire: Clarifies and sizes 200k writes/s.
  • Strong hire: Separates ephemeral live path from the batch pipeline, handles offline and safety.

questions.contextHtml:
Segment s_9 (a famous climb) has 9.8M efforts. Redis key segment:9:alltime uses ZADD LT elapsedS athlete to keep each athlete's best time. A matcher bug (v41) matched a car-accelerating route and wrote 2,300 impossible times (under 60 s for a 4 km climb) before it was fixed in v42. After the fix, the impossible times are still at the top. The same key uses about 1 GB of memory on a shared Redis.

ZRANGE segment:9:alltime 0 2 WITHSCORES -> athlete 8812 41, athlete 9120 44, athlete 2210 52
efforts table: those rows are marked invalid=true since the v42 fix
questions.promptHtml: Why are bad times still there, and how do you correct and harden the leaderboard?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ZREM the three entries" and move on.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the efforts table the source of truth? Do we have the second-best valid effort for these athletes? How many segments were affected?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hide the segment's leaderboard top entries from the API (excluded list) while repairing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: ZADD LT only lowers a score, so after the bad low value is written a correct larger value can never replace it; invalidating in SQL did not touch Redis.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare Redis against SELECT athlete, min(elapsedS) FROM efforts WHERE segment_id=9 AND invalid=false GROUP BY athlete.
  5. Root cause: Redis leaderboard is a cache with a one-way update rule; the correction happened only in the source of truth.
  6. Fix: Rebuild the key from the efforts table for affected segments: write to a new key with ZADD bulk load, atomically RENAME over the old one. Do it for every segment touched by v41 (found via efforts with that pipeline version), throttled so Redis stays responsive. Long-term: keep a repair job triggered by effort.invalidated events, and a periodic reconciliation of top entries against SQL.
  7. Prevention: Plausibility checks (speed limits per sport), flagging, a sanity alert when a record improves by more than a threshold, and tiering: very popular segments in a dedicated Redis, others in a database.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not ZREM by hand across thousands of segments; I would not trust LT for correctness when invalidation exists. A 10M-member set is about 1 GB, so keep it off shared nodes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rebuild takes minutes while reads continue? -> Build the new key then RENAME; readers see old or new, never partial.
  • Per-year and friends variants? -> Separate keys rebuilt from the same table, or computed from smaller sets at read time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A matcher bug planted fake records on hundreds of famous climbs; support spent weeks removing them one by one until a rebuild-from-ledger job existed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Manual ZREM.
  • Hire: Rebuilds from the efforts table and RENAMEs.
  • Strong hire: Understands LT one-way semantics, event-driven repair, plausibility checks and memory isolation.
